Methods for Sampling and Test for Petroleum and Related Products of Natural or Synthetic Origin (Excluding 
Bitumen) Sectional Committee, PCD 01 


FOREWORD 


This Indian Standard (Part 102) (First Revision) was adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards, after the draft 
finalized by the Methods for Sampling and Test for Petroleum and Related Products of Natural or Synthetic Origin 
(Excluding Bitumen) Sectional Committee had been approved by the Petroleum, Coal and Related Products 
Division Council. 


This standard provides a test method to determine the time the entrapped air requires to escape from the lubricant. 
Air release value, a critical property, can provide helpful information on the life of lubricated surfaces prone to 
surface pitting. 


This standard was first published in 1981. The first revision was brought out to keep pace with the latest 
technological developments and international practices. In this revision following major changes have been made: 


a) Additional information regarding lubricant viscosity for the selection of test temperature has been 
incorporated. 


In the preparation of this standard, considerable assistance has been derived from the joint publication of 
ASTM D 3427-15 and IP designation 313-01 “Standard test method for air release properties of hydrocarbon- 
based oil’. 


The composition of the Committee responsible for the formulation of this standard is given in Annex A. 


In reporting the result of a test or analysis made in accordance with this standard, if the final value, observed or 
calculated, is to be rounded off, it shall be done in accordance with IS 2 : 2022 ‘Rules for rounding off numerical 
values (second revision)’. 


IS 1448 (Part 102) : 2023 


Indian Standard 
METHODS OF TEST FOR PETROLEUM AND ITS PRODUCTS 
PART 102 DETERMINATION OF AIR RELEASE VALUE 


( First Revision ) 


1 SCOPE 


This standard prescribes the method of test for 
measurement of the ability of an oil to separate 
entrained air. It is generally applied to hydraulic and 
turbine oils but can also be applied to other 
lubricating oils. It can also be used for petroleum- 
based lubricants and synthetic fluids such as 
phosphate esters. 


2 TERMINOLOGY 


2.1 Air Release Value — The number of minutes 
required to reduce the air entrained in the oil to 
0.2 percent by volume under the conditions of this 
test and at the specified temperature. 


3SUMMARY OF METHOD 


3.1 Compressed air is passed through the test oil, 
which is heated to a temperature of 25 °C, 50 °C or 
75 °C € 0.1 °C. The test temperature for the oil shall 
be selected based on its viscosity at 40 °C as detailed 
below: 


a) The oils with a viscosity less than 9.0 cSt 
shall be tested at 25 ?C; 

b) The oils with a viscosity between 9.0 cSt and 
90.0 cSt shall be tested at 50 ?C; and 

c) The oils with a viscosity greater than 
90.0 cSt shall be tested at 75 °C + 0.1 °C. 


3.2 After the airflow is stopped, the time required for 
the air entrained in the oil to reduce in volume to 
0.2 percent is recorded. 


4 APPARATUS 


4.1 The apparatus, shown in Fig. 1, consists of the 
following: 


THERMOMETER 


<

REDUCING

FIG. 1 ASSEMBLY OF APPARATUS 


4.2 Test Vessel 


The test vessel, made of borosilicate glass, is shown 
in Fig. 2. It consists of a jacketed sample tube fitted 
with an air-inlet capillary, baffle plate and an air- 
outlet tube. The two parts of each test vessel should 
be labelled and always used as a pair. However, the 
parts can be interchanged if the resultant test vessel 
conforms to the stated dimensions. 


4.3 Pressure Gauge 


It should be capable of measuring the pressure in the 
range of 0 kPa to 35.5 kPa. 


4.4 Thermometer 


It should be capable of measuring the temperature 
from 0 °C to 100 °C in 0.2 °C intervals. 


NOTE — A thermometer conforming to the requirements 
of IP 64C is suitable for this test. 


4.5 Heater 


It is used to bring the compressed air temperature to 
the measurement temperature. A coil of copper 
tubing immersed in the circulating bath (see 4.7) is 
suitable at 25 °C, but additional heating is necessary 
at 50 °C and 75 °C. The test temperature can be 
achieved by an additional bath or using a separate 
steam or electric heat exchanger. The air 
temperature is measured by a thermometer meeting 
the specification mentioned in 4.4. 


4.6 Compressed Air 


Air from a cylinder or a non-pulsating pump can be 
used. However, it should be free from moisture and 
oil. 


4.7 Circulating Bath — Approximately 10 litre 
capacity with a flow rate of 10 l/min and capable of 
maintaining the test cell at a temperature of 25 °C, 
50 °C, or 75 °C within + 0.1 °C 


4.8 Density Balance 


It should be accurate to 0.000 5 g/ml, with round 
bottomed or tapered sinker with 5 ml or 10 ml 
displacement, 80.0 mm + 1.5 mm length. If the 
sinker contains a temperature, it shall be usable 
between 25 °C and 75 °C.

4.9 Oven — Capable of controlling temperatures up 
to 100 °C 


4.10 Timer — Readable to 1 s, with an accuracy of 
better than 0.1 percent 


5. REAGENTS 
5.1 Chrome Sulphuric Acid 


Dissolve 50 g of potassium dichromate in 1 litre of 
concentrated sulphuric acid (98 percent) and store in 
a glass bottle with a ground-glass stopper. 


CAUTION — This solution is strongly acidic and is 
a powerful oxidizing agent. Protective clothing, 
including an eye/face shield, should be worn when 
it is handled. Splashes on the skin should be 
immediately and thoroughly washed with water. 


5.2 1,1,1-trichloroethane 


CAUTION —  1,1,1-trichloroethane produces 
highly toxic fumes when heated to decomposition. 


5.3 Acetone — see IS 170 
6 PREPARATION OF APPARATUS 


Before each measurement, clean the interior of the 
test vessel, including the air inlet and sinker, and all 
other glassware coming in contact with the sample. 
First, rinse away the oil residue with 
1,1,1-trichloroethane and dry by air blowing. Clean 
the apparatus by immersing it in Chrome Sulphuric 
acid for a minimum of 12 hto remove any traces of 
silicone. Rinse with distilled water until the 
washings are acid-free, then rinse with acetone and 
dry with clean compressed air. 


7 PROCEDURE 


7.1 Assemble the test apparatus as shown in Fig. 1 
and set the circulating bath to the test temperature. 


7.2 Warm 200 ml of the oil to be tested in an oven 
set at a temperature of 10 *C higher than the test 
temperature. 


7.3 Pour 180 ml of the warmed sample into the test 
vessel. 


7.4 Allow the sample to reach the test temperature. 
It may take about 20 min. 


7.5 Warm the sinker of the density balance to the test 
temperature in an air bath, such as a glass cylinder 
fitted with a suitable cover situated in the circulating 
bath. When the sinker has reached the test 
temperature, immerse it in the sample, ensuring no 


IS 1448 (Part 102) : 2023 


air bubbles cling to it. Attach the sinker to the beam 
of the density balance using the platinum wire so 
that the bottom of the sinker is 10 mm + 2 mm above 
the bottom of the test vessel. 


7.6 Allow the density reader to stabilize, read the 
density from the balance to the nearest 0.001 g/ml 
and record it as the initial density, do. 


7.7 Return the sinker to the air bath and replace it 
with the air-inlet tube, as shown in Fig. 2. After 
5 min, start the air supply at a gauge pressure of 
20 kPa at the test temperature. Maintain the pressure 
and temperature by readjustments, if necessary. 


7.8 After 7 min, shut off the air and quickly remove 
the inlet tube from the test vessel. Immediately start 
the timer and set up the balance in its original 
position to the cell. Immense the sinker in the oil/air 
dispersion and attach the wire to the beam 
(see Note). 


NOTE — In the case of certain oils which form a 
considerable volume of oil/air dispersion, the top of the 
sinker may initially be in foam, and hence, density readings 
may be in error. 


7.9 Change the balance setting to 0.2 percent of air 
by volume (d-0.001 7), and record the time from 
shutting off the gas until the balance passes the null 
point. When using a direct reading density balance, 
record the time for the balance to reach d,-0.001 7. 
If the null point is not reached within 30 min, 
discontinue the test (see Note). 


NOTE — The value of 0.001 7 g/ml refers to oil of density 
0.850. For other densities, this value changes by 0.000 1 for 
each 0.05 change in density, that is, it will be 0.001 6 at 
0.800 and 0.002 0 at 1.000. 


7.10 Alternatively, where the air release-time curve 
is required, proceed as follows. After 1 min from the 
time the air is shut off, read and record the density 
to the nearest 0.001 g/ml as d;, and after that at 60 s 
intervals until the value do-0.001 g/ml is reached. If 
the time for separation exceeds 15 min, continue to 
read the density but at intervals of 5 min up to a total 
of 30 min, maximum. 


7.11 Plot a curve of density against time. The time 
at which the sample reaches 0.2 percent volume of 
entrained air can then be read directly from the graph 
and is given by do-0.001 7 g/ml. 


8 REPORT 


Report the air release value at (temperature) °C. 
Time up to 15 min shall be recorded to the nearest 
0.1 min and those from 15 min to 30 min to the 
nearest minutes. 


IS 1448 (Part 102) : 2023 


9 PRECISION 


9.1 The following precision data, reproduced from 
the German Standard DIN 51381 and ASTM 
D3427, may be used for judging the acceptability of 
the results (95 percent confidence). 


9.1.1 Repeatability 


Duplicate results by the same operator should not be 
considered suspect unless they differ by more than 
the amounts shown in the table under 9.1.2. 


9.1.2 Reproducibility 


The results submitted by each of the two laboratories 
should not be considered suspect unless they differ 


by more than the amounts shown in the following 
table:

Review of Indian Standards 


Amendments are issued to standards as the need arises on the basis of comments. Standards are also reviewed 
periodically; a standard along with amendments is reaffirmed when such review indicates that no changes are 
needed; if the review indicates that changes are needed, it is taken up for revision. Users of Indian Standards 
should ascertain that they are in possession of the latest amendments or edition by referring to the website-
